content: Gorse, also known as Ulex, is a genus of approximately 20 species of evergreen shrubs belonging to the subfamily Faboideae within the pea family Fabaceae. These plants are native to western Europe and northwest Africa, with the majority of species found in the Iberian Peninsula. Other common names for gorse include furze, whin, and furse. Gorse is closely related to broom plants and shares similar characteristics, such as green stems and very small leaves, which make it well-adapted to dry growing conditions. However, gorse is distinguished by its extreme spiny nature, with its leaves modified into spines that are 1–4 cm long. All gorse species produce yellow flowers, and some species have an extended flowering season. The most widely recognized species is Common Gorse (Ulex europaeus), which is native to most of western Europe. It typically grows in sunny locations, often on dry, sandy soils. Another species, Western Gorse (Ulex gallii), is characteristic of highly exposed Atlantic coastal heathlands and montane habitats. Common Gorse flowers most prominently in spring, although it can produce flowers year-round, giving rise to the old saying, When gorse is out of blossom, kissing's out of fashion. The flowers are noted for their strong, distinctive coconut-like scent. Western Gorse, also known as Dwarf Furze, differs in that it primarily flowers in late summer (August–September in Ireland and Britain) and has slightly darker yellow flowers compared to Common Gorse. Gorse is a fire-adapted plant, thriving in environments with stand-replacing fires. It is highly flammable, and its seed pods are often opened by fire, facilitating rapid regeneration. Burnt stumps can also sprout new growth from the roots. In the absence of fire, gorse tends to be shaded out by taller-growing trees unless other factors, such as exposure, prevent this. Fire recurrence periods in gorse stands typically range from 5 to 20 years. Gorse is valuable for wildlife, providing dense, thorny cover that is ideal for protecting bird nests. In Britain, France, and Ireland, it is particularly noted for supporting species such as European Stonechats and Dartford Warblers. The flowers are sometimes consumed by the larvae of the Double-striped Pug moth, and another moth species, Coleophora albicosta, feeds exclusively on Ulex. In many regions, including North America, southern South America, Australia, and New Zealand, Common Gorse was introduced as an ornamental plant but has since become naturalized and invasive due to its aggressive seed dispersal. It is notoriously difficult to eradicate. However, in New Zealand, gorse has been found to serve as a useful nursery species for native bush regeneration. When gorse stands are left undisturbed for several years, native seedlings can grow in their shelter, eventually outcompeting and replacing the gorse by cutting off its access to light. Gorse flowers are edible and can be used in salads, brewed into tea, or fermented to produce a non-grape-based wine. The furze is also the badge of the MacLennan clan from Kintail, Scotland, and Furse is a surname associated with Devon.
